description:
I was fairly amazed to see that Baltimore Orioles and Orchard Orioles seem to  tolerate each other without territorial squabbles - or at least I've not seen any evidence of disputes. 

This beautiful male Baltimore Oriole was happily singing in this tree that is on the site of the ruined foundations of a small barn about six meters above a tributary of Buffalo Creek. 

After I took the first of these photos I listened to Yellow Warblers, Common Yellowthroats, and American Redstarts singing, mostly just out of sight, for fifteen minutes, when I heard, saw, photographed, and recorded a male Orchard Oriole singing for a few minutes in this same tree! 

Just *five minutes* after the Orchard Oriole flew on, I took the second of these photos of the same (or another?) Baltimore Oriole back in the very same tree. They were just taking turns in this popular spot. Is that usual? Do these two species just get along really well? It's fantastic to see them both practically together in any case. 

Unfortunately, five days later, a male Baltimore Oriole was found dead on the road not far away. I can't quite imagine how that happens - a car killing a songbird on a fairly quiet rural road. Speeding? Sad.

Baltimore Oriole (Icterus galbula) is a medium-size, migratory songbird in the New World Blackbirds and Orioles (Icteridae) family. Orioles are usually seen in the vicinity of tall palm trees because they weave their nests behind the dead palm fronds. Orioles are sometimes called "palm-leaf Orioles," because they "sew" their hanging nests onto the undersides of palm fronds. These nests are almost never visible from below. That’s why old palm fronds should never be cut down from the palm trees--to help preserve Oriole habitat.
